newsitem.title: GERMANY: Taboo lifted, German troops prepare for Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Taboo lifted, German troops prepare for Bosnia.

text.p: Clad in combat fatigues and with a rifle strapped over his shoulder, Corporal Andreas Heim said he could not understand the fuss over the first mission abroad for German combat troops since World War Two.
Born 25 years after that war ended, Heim said it was about time the German military shed its postwar shackles to help, if only in a small way, to secure the peace in Bosnia.
"Germany is one of the leading economic nations in the world so why should we stand on the sidelines?" asked Heim, 26, at this remote army base 100 km (60 miles) east of Frankfurt.
NATO commanders in Sarajevo on Friday formally launched the multi-national Stabilisation Force, taking over from the Implementation Force (IFOR), to police the Dayton peace accord.
Heim and about 3,300 other German soldiers will join the NATO-led SFOR in January.
"We are contributing to security in Europe," said Heim, his baby face strapped tightly into a heavy combat helmet. "Germany cannot hide behind its past any more."
The German army will be sending the third-largest SFOR contingent to Bosnia after the U.S. and Britain.

It will include 2,000 infantry and armoured vehicle-borne reconnaissance troops equipped and trained for combat -- a deployment that was for decades unthinkable in a country whose history was so tarnished by its menacing military.

The Bosnian deployment has attracted surprisingly little dissent in Germany and has been applauded abroad in capitals that have long called on Bonn to contribute manpower. It was also overwhelmingly approved by parliament this month.
The soldiers in Volkach, a windswept training centre in the hills of central Germany, are more concerned about Bosnian minefields than any lingering fears of German soldiers abroad.
"Times have changed," said Lieutenant Colonel Andreas Becker, 34, a bomb disposal expert headed for Sarajevo, reflecting on the absence of protest from German pacifists.
Seasoned career professionals, the German soldiers sound proud to be part of the peacekeeping force.

"It seemed clear to me that as soon as the Americans started reducing their forces in Europe after the Cold War ended, we Germans would have to carry more weight," said Bernd Ludwicziek, a 29-year-old drill sergeant.
"This sort of peacekeeping mission is something that should be normal for the Bundeswehr," Ludwicziek added.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe have succeeded in chiseling away at the strong pacificist streak left behind by Germany's ignominious militaristic past.
"I am delighted for the Bundeswehr that this has become normal," Ruehe said during a inspection tour here. "It is very important for the army and a tribute to their achievements."

In a country with deep scars left by the Nazis and wary of its Prussian heritage, the question of sending soldiers abroad had for five decades been answered by political leaders and the broader population with just one word: "Nein!"
After unification in 1990, Kohl moved forward with a series of small steps to lift the taboo on German deployments abroad.
One reason was Germany's humiliation in 1991 when it paid $5.5 billion to Western Allies fighting Iraq in the Gulf rather than send even a token force to aid in Kuwait's liberation.
An important milestone came in 1992, when Germany sent manpower and equipment to U.N.-backed missions -- a field hospital in Cambodia and back-up support in Somalia in 1993.
